Rock bottom: you come up with enough gas for a stressed diver and their rescuer, and never below 50 bar. It is what most training teaches. It is not enough when you must come back the way you went.
Reserve: you finish the dive with the bar you set. It is not enough when the way back is longer than the way out.
Ascent pressure: you start up when the cylinder reaches the pressure you set.

Model: a 3 min stop at 5 m; rock bottom at twice the combined gas use for 1 minute, an ascent no faster than 9 m/min and 10 bar; air and nitrox 21 to 40 % to 40 m; real gas in the cylinder.

Rock bottom: you go up when the gas left is what two divers need to reach the surface from that depth, both breathing at twice their normal rate for one minute, then a direct ascent at 9 m/min, plus 10 bar. Never below 50 bar here. Taught by UTD and GUE; Subsurface and GasPlanner calculate it too.
It needs your real SAC. It assumes the problem happens at that depth and says nothing about a long swim back.
Fixed reserve: you finish the dive with this much left in the cylinder, so the ascent and the safety stop are counted on top. Dive centres and agencies teach a fixed reserve, from about 30 to 50 bar.
A fixed number ignores depth: at 30 m it is well below rock bottom, at 12 m it is generous.
Fixed ascent pressure: you start going up when the gauge reaches this pressure. “Up at 100 bar” is a common dive-centre rule.
A fixed number ignores depth and group size; compare it with rock bottom, which is always shown.
Halves: half the gas for the way out, half for the way back. Taught for dives that return the way they went. In a group the smaller supply decides how many litres are spent before turning.
It leaves nothing in reserve: not enough for trouble on an open-water ascent.
Thirds: a third out, a third back, a third in reserve. Taught for cave and wreck diving. In a group the smaller supply decides how many litres are spent before turning.
Sixths: a sixth out, a sixth back, the rest kept. Used for demanding overhead dives where the way back is long or slow. In a group the smaller supply decides how many litres are spent before turning.
For overhead diving with training; it is not a rule for open water.
